ww.Mulberry molars: Mulberry molars are also a late sign of congenital syphilis, but they affect the first permanent molar, whose chewing surface has crowded, poorly formed cusps. Here the abnormal teeth are the central incisors, with notched biting edges.
ww.Dental fluorosis: Dental fluorosis comes from excess fluoride during tooth formation and leaves white, mottled or brown enamel on teeth of normal shape. Here the problem is the shape of the incisors, which are narrow and notched.
ww.Tetracycline staining: Tetracycline staining gives teeth of normal shape a yellow-brown or gray color, in bands, when the drug is taken while the teeth are forming. Here the incisors differ in shape, being narrow and notched, and no color change defines them.
ww.Amelogenesis imperfecta: Amelogenesis imperfecta is an inherited enamel defect that makes the enamel thin, pitted or soft across many teeth. Here only the central incisors are abnormal, and their defining feature is a notch in the biting edge.

look: Look at the two central incisors in the middle of the arch. Instead of a straight, flat biting edge, each is narrow and has a shallow notch in its biting edge, and a small gap separates them. These are permanent teeth, so the sign appears years after birth. Notched central incisors with a gap between them are Hutchinson teeth, a late sign of congenital syphilis.

findings: Notched central incisors: the two central incisors at the top center are narrow, and the biting edge of each has a shallow notch or scalloped dip instead of a straight edge. This notching is the hallmark of Hutchinson teeth.
Gap between incisors: a small gap separates the two central incisors at the midline, so the teeth look narrow and widely spaced, unlike the broad, touching incisors of normal permanent teeth.

Permanent teeth: these are permanent incisors, so Hutchinson teeth are a late finding of untreated congenital syphilis, seen once the permanent incisors erupt in childhood. They form part of the Hutchinson triad with interstitial keratitis and deafness.

ann.l: The two central incisors have a shallow notch or crescent-shaped dip in the biting edge instead of a straight, flat edge. Infection during tooth development disrupts the forming enamel, so the permanent incisor erupts with this notched shape.

A prominent central gap (diastema) separates the narrow, peg-shaped central incisors. Because the teeth taper towards their biting edges rather than widening normally, broad spacing remains between them instead of normal interproximal contact.

These changes affect the permanent dentition, making Hutchinson teeth a late manifestation of congenital syphilis that becomes evident only upon tooth eruption in childhood. They represent one component of Hutchinson's classic triad, alongside Eighth nerve deafness and interstitial keratitis.
